extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/natural history/sociology interested in general theory of evolution (educated general readership)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing evolution from indefinite to definite
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the author's conceptual criteria for recognizing and characterizing evolutionary change (material and dynamical) across biology, society, language, science, arts, and technical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution involves a progress from the indeterminate (indefinite) to the determinate (definite) — both in particular forms and in groups of forms (species, genera, orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: lowest organisms (Protozoa, sponges) exhibit extreme indefiniteness of shape and variable structure, while highest organisms show precise, invariable attributes and proportions. If complex organisms arose from simpler ones by accumulated modifications, an increase of definiteness must have accompanied that evolution. (See §§133–134.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress from homogeneity to heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: A general trait of evolution is change from an (indefinite, incoherent) homogeneity to a (definite, coherent) heterogeneity, accompanying dissipation of motion and integration of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's modified formula: evolution is 'a change from an indefinite, incoherent homogeneity, to a definite coherent heterogeneity, accompanying the dissipation of motion and integration of matter.' This frames definiteness as linked to increasing heterogeneity and integration (§138).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence and disappearance of intermediate forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolutionary development involves divergence of lineages so contrasts between groups increase and intermediate (less well-adapted) forms disappear, producing distinct and stable species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism and illustration: natural selection produces tendency to divergence; less fit intermediate forms vanish, leaving sharply marked species and higher taxa. This is used to explain increased distinctness between species, genera, orders (§133).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social differentiation and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies progress from indeterminate, loosely organized tribes to more definite organizations with settled territorial boundaries, clearly separated social classes, distinct occupational divisions, and defined priesthoods or authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: primitive wandering tribes versus mature nations; rise of territorial limits, separation of warrior, industrial, and priest classes; Egypt, Assyria, India, China cited as exemplars of pronounced social definiteness. Also noted: social metamorphosis can temporarily blur old distinctions while new ones form (§134).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional consolidation via rules and precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: All organized social results (religious, charitable, literary societies, legislation) gain definiteness as accumulated rules, precedents, and interpretations elaborate vague ends and modes into specific, restricted practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process and consequence: new laws begin vague and are elaborated into specific clauses and judicial interpretations; accumulation of rules makes purposes more distinct but may ultimately lead to fixity and inability to adapt (decay) (§134).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic precision through grammatical and lexical elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages evolve increasing precision by adding grammatical markers (inflections, adjectives, adverbs) and by multiplying lexical terms; these narrow meanings and permit more exact communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: undeveloped tongues with mostly nouns/verbs are vague; addition of inflections and words limits conditions of action/existence; multiplication of terms reduces semantic range; dictionaries and settled definitions further fix meaning (§135).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific progress from qualitative to quantitative knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Science advances from qualitative, vague relations to precisely classified and quantified relations, enabling exact inference about antecedents and consequents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: geometric theorems arranged by Euclid, methods of limits in calculus, progressively more accurate astronomical predictions (errors reduced from days to seconds), chemical analysis of compounds, physiological measurement (spirometer, sphygmograph), statistical methods in pathology and sociology (§136).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic and literary fidelity to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine arts and literature show evolutionary progress toward more accurate representation of reality: increased precision in form, individuality in characters, and rejection of improbable/supernatural contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative examples: rudely-carved idols and medieval mural paintings vs later Greek sculpture and modern painting; romantic/miraculous medieval plots contrasted with modern novels and plays praised for fidelity to individual character and plausibility (§137).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical precision in tools and manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial evolution produces increased accuracy and precision in artifacts and machinery as techniques and specialized tools (planing machines, dividing-engines, micrometers, microscopes) are developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: contrast between ancient/aboriginal tools and modern instruments; planing machines enable truly straight lines and air-tight surfaces; named instruments (Troughton's dividing-engine, Whitworth micrometer) demonstrate vastly improved accuracy (§137).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness as secondary to consolidation and separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased definiteness is not primary but an incidental result of other changes: as wholes concentrate and parts separate from environment and from one another, outlines become sharper and parts more distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: consolidation draws peripheral portions into masses, completing disunion from neighboring portions; definiteness accompanies increasing consolidation and heterogeneity, rather than being the primary driver (§138).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of motions (dynamical aspect of evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: As material aggregates form and parts consolidate, retained (non-escaping) motion becomes integrated and differentiated into sensible, rhythmical motions; concrete motions of masses arise from aggregation of diffused molecular motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process and examples: molecular motion gives rise to motions of gases, liquids, solids, vegetation growth, animal movement; stored/retained motion in aggregates permits secondary redistributions and generation of new integrated motions (see §§139–140).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between structural heterogeneity and motion heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneities in size, form, and quality of parts necessarily produce heterogeneities in amounts and directions of their motions; increasing structural definiteness implies increasing definiteness of motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication and consequence: as parts segregate and consolidate, their relative mobilities change and rhythmical actions differentiate alongside structural differentiation (§139).

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased multiformity of rhythms with higher aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each new order of aggregation tends to generate new orders of rhythm (varied periodicities and motions); increased multiformity of arrangement produces increased multiformity of rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical illustrations: molecules of different gases have different undulation rates; solar-system formation yields planets/satellites with unlike periods and rotations; aggregate complexity creates complex but still definite rhythms and motions (§140–141).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculability and definite complexity arising from integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Though complexity increases, integrated systems yield definite, calculable motions and predictable relations (periods, perturbations, secular variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: integrated motions of the Solar System become mutually dependent and calculable; secular and periodic variations form an integrated set of movements whose results can be calculated despite complexity (§140).
